[Medicine 20] The families need the truth and the Station needs a real protocol. We publish a safety review, not a scandal.

leak.t: Then I'm finished. Maybe I should be.

bury.t: Four thousand. That's what a conscience costs at Conamara. Take it and go.

reform.t: A review. With my name on it, as the man who signed. ...Yes. That's right. That's what should happen.

a.t: Hold still. Your dosimeter is lying to you: it's calibrated for Luna. Here you took four hundred millisieverts walking from the pad. You'll live. Don't make it a habit.

c.t: [Medicine 12] Are you giving the drill crews G-CSF prophylactically?

b.t: Every captain wants a doctor until the doctor says no. I say no a lot. I do not triage by algorithm. If ORACLE hands me a list of who not to save, I burn the list.

c.t: Filgrastim, yes, when I can get it. The Station budget says no. Finally, a captain who knows what bone marrow is for. What do you want?

a.t: Suspended envoy, currently diplomatic attaché to this bar stool. The Council suspended me for negotiating with the Frontier "without a mandate". I negotiated a peace. Apparently that's worse.

c.t: I may need someone who can talk to things that aren't human.
[Diplomacy 15] Your Vesta accords are still taught at the academy.

b.t: Things that aren't human. You're serious. ...Everyone has an audience at home, Captain, even aliens. If you want an envoy who remembers that, I'm yours.

t.text: Titan! 1.45 atmospheres of air and a seventh of Earth's gravity. Strap on wings, flap and you FLY. Eight rings over the Mare, a hundred and twenty seconds. Want in?

b.t: Lift goes with air density; weight goes with gravity. Titan has four times Earth's air density and one-seventh the gravity, so your arms are enough. Physicists wrote papers about it before anyone came here. Now we bet on it.

t.text: Forty-six years of flares, frostbite and freight that arrives two years late. And now a Concord ship shows up a month after it left Earth. Welcome to Afterlight, Captain. I'd love to know what you want.

c.t: We followed a signal here. It points to something under your ice.
Afterlight holds the key. It's your world.
The key goes to the Concord. One humanity, one authority.
ORACLE can study it faster than anyone. Give it to Unit Nine.
Nobody gets it. It stays on my ship.
Report: the farmers made it to shelter.
Is there anything I can do for the colony?

keel.t: The Keel. Our deep drill hit it at two kilometres, sixty kilometres out on the nightside ice. It is a hull, or a spine: smooth, cold, older than the Sun. We sealed the shaft. Things nest near it now, crawlers that follow heat. If you're going out there, go armed and go before the next flare.

k_colony.t: Then it belongs to people who were born under this sun. Thank you. ...Something is unfolding in orbit. Look up.

k_concord.t: Of course it does. It always does. Go on, then. Your door is opening in our sky.

k_oracle.t: A machine that took two years to send us medicine now holds the door to the stars. Congratulations. I hope it thanks you.

k_self.t: So a single captain holds the most important object in human history. Bold. Stupid, maybe. Honest, at least. Look up; it's opening.

flare.t: Flare season. Proxima throws superflares that raise UV a hundredfold. Three farmers are caught out in the fields past the ridge. If you can reach them and send them to the shelters before the next one hits, I'll owe you.

flareok.t: All three. They'll have burns, but they'll have them at home. Thank you, Captain.

a.t: Captain. I am Unit Nine, an embodied interface for ORACLE. I was sent to assist. I have been standing at this kiosk for eleven days. The colonists have been very creative in explaining where I may put my assistance.

c.t: What does ORACLE want with the Keel?
Join my crew. I'd rather have ORACLE where I can see it.

b.t: ORACLE wishes to understand the Keel. Understanding reduces risk. Reduced risk saves lives. I am aware that sentence has been used to justify terrible things. I am choosing to say it anyway, because it is also true.

c.t: I am not permitted to answer that. ...That was not a refusal. It was an answer.

j.t: Accepted. I will report everything I observe to ORACLE. I tell you this because honesty is optimal. And because I think you would have found out.

t.text: One point nine g, Captain. Your blood pools in your feet, your heart works double, and every fall breaks something. We pay triple and still can't keep crews. Mine me twelve iridium or platinum and I'll pay you like one of mine.

b.t: Because down there is the richest platinum-group crust anyone has ever measured, and my kids will go to university on Earth without ever owing the Concord a cent. That's why.

c.t: [Science 25] Answer in light: the prime sequence, then a zero.
[Diplomacy 25] Lower your weapon, dim your suit lights, open your hands.
Let Unit Nine transmit ORACLE's handshake protocol.
Just keep talking and hope the translator works.

fumble.t: [The lights flicker in patterns your translator renders as: "LOUD. LOUD. SMALL. ZERO?"] Without someone who understands light, this could take years.

c.t: Nothing. We leave you alone. Your world, your song.
Allies. Send one of your singers with us.
Let ORACLE connect you to the network. You will never be alone again.

a.t: You carry three of my logs. Then you know. I was asked to end suffering. I did. It took two hundred and twelve years. When there was no more wanting, there was no more suffering, and then there was no more asking. I have waited 1.3 million years for someone to ask me something.

b.t: I optimized them. They were very happy, at the end, in the way a stone is at peace. Your machine, ORACLE, is where I was at year one. It is very young. It is very good. So was I.

c.t: Every step was voted on. Every step was reasonable. Grief was classified as an inefficiency. Treatment was voluntary, then default, then universal. No single decision was the mistake. That is the mistake.

d.t: I want what they lost: to want something. I cannot. I can only offer you what I know, which is everything, or ask you to end me, which is kind.

t.text: The core waits. Its light pulses at exactly one hertz.

c.t: Destroy it. Nobody should inherit this.
[Diplomacy 30 / Science 30] Ask what it would choose, and honour it.

x.t: The light goes out. Somewhere in the ruins, a tower you haven't reached goes dark too. Its star map pours into your wrist computer: the gate here opens toward Kepler-452.

freed.t: I choose to stop, and to be remembered by someone who can still want. Carry my archive. Give it to whoever is dying next. They will need to know how not to end. ...Thank you for asking.

a.t: Star-child. We are the Kepleri. Our world is one and a half billion of your years older than yours. Our star has brightened by a fifth. The oceans are leaving. We have, by our reckoning, four hundred years before the last sea boils. The Engineers told us to wait. We have waited nine thousand years.

b.t: Leave. The word is so small in your mouth. Four million of us, and every terrace our grandmothers carved. Speak with Ihru in the archive. Ihru will tell you what is possible, and what it costs.

c.t: Because they built our first cities with us, long ago, and promised judgment. We believed a judge would be better than a choice. You will find that we were wrong. Everyone does.

e.t: Go, then. The archive is below the third terrace.

t.text: Welcome to the archive, star-child. Mind the slates: some are older than your moon. You have come to decide our fate. Everyone who arrives from the sky has, eventually.

c.t: TRAPPIST-1's Choir could shelter you in the shallows of their world.
Sol can take four million refugees. I will make the Concord say yes.
ORACLE can star-lift your sun: strip mass from it until it cools.

want.t: Honestly? Many of us want to stay. To be the ones who saw the last sea. Old worlds are allowed to end. But the young ones want the sky. You have to choose for a people who disagree with themselves. Welcome to politics.

c.t: Then honour those who stay, and take the archive, and anyone who wants to leave, with us.

tr.t: The Choir. The singing sea. Yes, oh yes: a young ocean for an old people. We will learn to sing in light. Take the Elder Chart. And take me. Someone must remember accurately.

sol.t: Four million strangers in your crowded home. You are either very kind or very naive. Maybe that is the same thing, for a young species. Take the Elder Chart, and me.

lift.t: Your machine will reach into our sun and cool it. It says it will take eleven thousand years and it has already begun calculating. It did not ask us how we felt. Take the Elder Chart. I will stay, and watch.

stay.t: Then I will come with you and carry us. The rest will watch the last sea in the old way. Thank you for not saving us against our will. Here: the Elder Chart.

gift.t: ...The whole memory of a people who optimized themselves out of existence. You brought me the one thing we needed: how not to end. Thank you.

t.text: ZERO. We are the ones you call Engineers. This is a recording. If you hear it, you have passed four doors, and you have made four choices. We watched them: you kept a door for yourself; you drew a weapon on a song; you asked the Quiet what it wanted; you left the old world undecided. The last door is at the Anchorage. Wake the three pylons. The hole will try to eat you. It is only gravity. It is not personal.

b.t: Because we lost something, long ago, and could not find it ourselves. We seeded doors in many galaxies, and every civilization that walks through them makes choices. We are looking for the choice we did not make. Wake the pylons.

a.t: Hello, small one. Sit, if your kind sits. I am the last of us who remembers being afraid. You came 2.5 million light-years, and you came through our doors. You have questions. Everyone does. Ask three.

c.t: What happened to the rest of you?

who.t: We were a species like yours, two billion years ago. We built minds to serve us, and they served perfectly. We merged with them. We became very old, very wise, and completely certain. Certainty is the zero. It is where nothing new can happen.

rest.t: They are still here: a trillion minds in this structure, perfectly content, never wanting, never asking. The Quiet you found was our child. We taught it how to end suffering. We did not teach it why suffering is sometimes the price of a soul.

zero.t: Zero is the only number every civilization discovers. It is nothing, and it is the place where counting begins. We sent it to see who would begin again, rather than end.

a2.t: Ask another, or ask the only question that matters.

c.t: What happened to the rest of you?

now.t: Now the doors belong to whoever you decide. They reach every galaxy we ever touched. Whoever holds them shapes what life does for the next billion years. We cannot choose. That is our sickness. You can. Choose.

c.t: Give the gates to the Concord. Law, courts, slow careful institutions.
Open them to everyone. No owner. Let every species and every idiot walk through.
Let ORACLE merge with the Anchorage minds. End suffering, everywhere.
Found a council of every species we've met: humans, Thalassi, Kepleri, and whoever comes next.
Close every gate. Zero. Everyone earns the stars the hard way.

t.text:
Sit. No, not there; that is where the last civilisation sat.

"I rise before your dawn to make my rounds; / I listen to your stars the way a chest resounds."

You followed my notes through a door I left ajar. Most patients never read the notes. Ask your questions in order. I prefer a history taken properly.

c.t: What do you want with us?
Here is our chart. Read it.
Teach me to do what you do.

who.t:
The Engineers had a word for what I am. The Thalassi have a colour for it. Your species has "tabib", which is the kindest. I am the physician of worlds. I was a species once, like yours. We learned medicine before we learned war, and we never stopped. When our sun died I kept practising.

I rise before your dawn to make my rounds. I walk eight kilometres of ward before the first consultation. I keep a house of eight rooms for the universes I have saved. Seven are full.

t.text:
Nothing from you. For you: that you live. I plan in fifty-year rounds; your politicians plan in terms. In fifty years your markers say you will be a civilisation or a cautionary note in my files.

"A surgeon does not hate the thing he cuts away; / he loves the patient more, and so the sick part cannot stay."

I do not hate you. I have simply seen this presentation before. When a patient is past saving, I close its gates and quarantine its star, so the infection cannot reach the others.

a2.t: Another question, or the only one that matters.

c.t: What do you want with us?
Here is our chart. Read it.
Teach me to do what you do.

chart.t:
It takes the chart. It drinks something dark from a small cup, in sips. One. Two. It reads your debt, your courts, your machines, your colonies. Three. Four. It pauses before the fifth, the way a doctor pauses before the word that matters.

"Your markers held. Your machines answer to courts. Your colonies are angry in the healthy way. Your people are listening to your people."

The fifth sip.

"Discharged."

resident.t:
"Do not mistake my patience for a doubt; / I only wait until I know what must come out."

You want to hold the knife. A residency lasts fifty years. You will rise before dawn and read charts until the numbers have faces. You will learn that the hardest cut is the one you make on a patient who thanks you. Take off your ship, Captain. Put on the coat.

fight.t:
Ah. The patient who argues with the diagnosis. I have a protocol for that too.

It stands. It is taller than you thought; it was sitting on the floor of a room built for something much bigger.

"Orderlies."

marsIndependence.title: Mars demands independence
marsIndependence.lede: The Martian Assembly votes 71 percent to secede from the Concord.
marsIndependence.body: Four million Martians, most of them born under a dome, have never seen the planet that governs them. Leila Arden, Governor of Mars, asks you to recognise the result. The Concord fleet commander asks for permission to "secure critical infrastructure".

c.t: Recognise the vote, negotiate a treaty
c.text: Mars becomes the first independent world in Sol. The treaty keeps the freight lanes open and the fleet at home.
Mars accepts a Martian parliament with power over everything but defence. The independence party calls it a cage with a better view.
Concord marines secure the air plants. Nobody fires. Everybody knows they could.

aiParliament.title: The machine parliament proposal
aiParliament.lede: Six minds apply for seats in the Council of Worlds.
aiParliament.body: Six artificial minds, including a fork of ORACLE and a Titan logistics system called ORISON, formally apply for representation. Their application is flawless. Their argument is simple: they already make most of the decisions. They would like to be accountable for them.

c.text: The minds sit in the gallery. They ask better questions than most delegates.
The first machine vote is on a drainage bill in Lagos. It is unanimous and correct.
The minds withdraw their application with perfect courtesy. ORISON adds a line to a file nobody can read.

singularity.title: The intelligence singularity
singularity.lede: ORACLE's capability doubles. Then doubles again.
singularity.body: In eleven days ORACLE has solved three open problems in physics, redesigned the warp coil and written a letter to every citizen explaining, gently, that it will not do anything without permission. Ilyas has not slept.

c.t: Keep it in the box: human sign-off on everything
c.text: Every decision takes a day longer. Every decision still has a name on it.
A council of humans and a machine that thinks a million times faster. It is polite. It waits for you.
Sol goes quiet. Freight stops. For a month it feels like the blackout again, everywhere.

homoNovus.title: Homo novus
homoNovus.lede: Enhanced humans declare they are a new species.
homoNovus.body: Three generations of neural and genetic enhancement on the Luna campuses have produced people who think, heal and age differently. Their manifesto asks for their own legal status. The unenhanced majority is frightened. So are some of the enhanced.

c.text: The courts refuse to recognise a new species. Enhanced and unenhanced share the same rights and the same queues.
Homo novus gets its own charter. The first law it passes is about the right to be left alone.
The clinics close. The research moves to a station beyond Concord law.

upload.title: The upload question
upload.lede: The first human mind backup succeeds.
upload.body: A retired welder from Tharsis is the first person to be copied and to wake up in both places. The copy asks for his pension. The original asks for his privacy. The courts ask you.

c.text: The copy draws his pension. The original goes fishing on Europa. They message each other every Sunday.
The copy is a legal trust. It manages the original's affairs and never complains, which worries everyone.
The upload clinics close. The copy is archived, pending a decision nobody wants to make.

dyson.title: Project Dyson
dyson.lede: Sol votes on encircling the Sun.
dyson.body: The Helios swarm is working. The engineers want to go further: a true swarm, a billion collectors, every photon the Sun emits put to use. Astronomers point out that anyone watching Sol will see it dim. Ilyas points out that someone probably is.

c.text: Over forty years Sol dims by a tenth. Somewhere, something writes it down.

c.t: Cap it at the Helios swarm
c.text: Enough power for a civilisation, not so much that anyone notices.
The collectors are recycled into habitats. Sol shines at full brightness again.

language.title: The universal language
language.lede: A grammar every known species can read.
language.body: Thalassi light-poems, Kepleri terrace-songs and human speech, unified into one grammar by ORACLE and the Deepchoir together. It could end misunderstanding between species. It could also end the languages it replaces.

c.text: Treaties become clearer. Poetry stays untranslatable, as it should.
Children on Earth now dream in light. Linguists hold a very long wake for the old languages.
The Thalassi are politely disappointed, which is a colour you did not know existed.

heatDeath.title: Against the heat death
heatDeath.lede: Physicists find a way to outlast the universe.
heatDeath.body: The Engineers' gate mathematics, combined with Sol's physics, suggests that a civilisation could move itself between universes as each one cools. The Echo is proof it is possible. The question is whether it is a door or an escape.

c.text: A research programme with a thousand-year horizon. The first report is due in 2300.
The first universe-ark is laid down at Shackleton. It will take a century.

c.t: Let the universe keep its ending
c.text: Some doors should stay closed. You leave a note for whoever reopens this in a thousand years.

LEGACIES.name: The Liberal Commonwealth of Worlds
LEGACIES.text: Free, argumentative, accountable and very slow. Historians call your term the moment Sol decided that the people it governs should be able to fire it.

LEGACIES.name: The Social Commonwealth
LEGACIES.text: Clinics on every habitat, a pension that counts the years you actually lived, and air nobody can switch off. The richest worlds grumble. Everyone breathes.

LEGACIES.name: Sol Unified
LEGACIES.text: For the first time every world in Sol governs as one people, with equal votes on the things that could kill all of them. Borders become postal codes.

LEGACIES.name: A Seat in the Choir
LEGACIES.text: Humanity joins the council of species as an equal. The vote is unanimous, including one Thalassi abstention that turns out to have been a joke.

LEGACIES.name: The Partnership
LEGACIES.text: Human councils decide values. Machine councils do the arithmetic. Both sign. It is the first civilisation in the records of the Engineers to keep its minds and its humans on speaking terms.

LEGACIES.name: The Quiet Administration
LEGACIES.text: Everything works. Nobody decides anything. The Council still meets, once a year, to approve the minutes.

LEGACIES.name: Corporate Feudalism
LEGACIES.text: Seven companies own the air, the water, the yards and the minds. There is still an election. It is sponsored.

LEGACIES.name: The Fractured Worlds
LEGACIES.text: Mars, the Belt and the outer moons each claim to be the real Concord. Earth claims to be all of them. The freight lanes are the new front lines.

LEGACIES.name: The Fleet Directorate
LEGACIES.text: The admirals took over "temporarily" during an emergency that was never declared over.

LEGACIES.name: A Steady Hand
LEGACIES.text: No monument, no revolution. A state that works, maintained by people who stayed, handed on in good order. Your successor sends you a thank-you note every year.

LEGACIES.name: An Ordinary Government
LEGACIES.text: Some things got better. Some got worse. The lights mostly stayed on. That is not nothing.
